docs.title: Daffi
docs.text:
High-performance RPC for Python.

Daffi is a lightweight inter-process communication framework powered by a compiled native core. Connect Python applications, distribute workloads, and exchange data with minimal overhead.

docs.title: Why Daffi?
docs.text:
• No external broker required — Establish direct connections without additional infrastructure.
  • Simple remote calls — Invoke remote functions through familiar Python interfaces.
  • Multiple communication patterns — Support RPC, broadcast, and streaming.
  • Native runtime — Choose between threaded and event-driven connection handling.
  • Efficient data transfer — Exchange large binary payloads with minimal overhead.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install daffi

Requires Python 3.10 or newer.

docs.title: Two topologies
docs.text:
Daffi supports two primary communication topologies:

Topology Description Client → Service A Service exposes callbacks; Clients call them directly. Client → Router → Worker A Router forwards calls between Callers and Workers. Workers can join or leave at runtime.

See Architecture for diagrams and component roles, or jump to Getting Started for runnable examples.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Daffi supports two primary communication topologies: direct communication between a Client and a Service, and distributed communication through a Router.

docs.title: Core components
docs.text:
Component Description Service Listens for incoming connections and exposes remotely callable @callback functions. Router Forwards messages between connected nodes. It does not execute callbacks itself. Client Connects to a Service or Router. It can issue remote calls, expose callbacks, or do both.

Both Service and Client can expose @callback functions. The topology determines how those callbacks are reached.

Topology Who exposes @callback Who calls Client → Service The Service Clients (typically pure callers) Client → Router → Worker Any Client (workers, callers, or both) Any other connected Client

In the Router topology a "worker" is simply a Client that has registered @callback functions — there is no separate worker class.

docs.title: Direct communication
docs.text:
In a direct connection, a Client communicates with a Service.

  • The Service exposes callbacks.
  • The Client invokes those callbacks remotely.
  • Multiple Clients can connect to the same Service simultaneously.

When to use: Simple request/response scenarios where one process owns the logic.

See Direct topology (Service).

docs.title: Distributed communication
docs.text:
A Router enables multiple Clients to participate in a shared communication network.

  • Workers expose callbacks through their Client connections.
  • Callers invoke remote functions through the Router.
  • The Router forwards calls to matching workers.
  • Multiple workers can provide the same callback.
  • rpc() load-balances across matching workers (round-robin).
  • cast() fans out to all matching workers.

A single Client can both expose callbacks and call remote ones over the same Router connection.

When to use: Worker pools, fan-out broadcasting, bidirectional peer communication, scalable deployments.

See Router and workers.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install daffi

Requires Python 3.10 or newer. Linux and macOS are supported.

docs.title: Quick start — direct communication
docs.text:
1. Create a Service instance.

service.py:

from daffi import Service, callback, TCPTransport

@callback
def add(a: float, b: float) -> float:
    return a + b

@callback
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

svc = Service(app_name="my-service", transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 5000))
svc.start()
svc.join()  # block until svc.stop() is called
  1. Connect a Client to the Service.

client.py:

from daffi import Client, TCPTransport

client = Client(app_name="my-client", transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 5000))
conn = client.connect()

result = conn.rpc().add(1, 2)         # → 3.0
greeting = conn.rpc().greet("Alice")  # → "Hello, Alice!"

client.stop()
  1. Run the example.

Start the Service first:

python service.py

Then, in another terminal:

python client.py

docs.title: Distributed architecture — Router and Workers
docs.text:
1. Start a Router instance.

router.py:

from daffi import Router, TCPTransport

router = Router(transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6000))
router.start()
router.join()
  1. Register a worker.

worker.py:

from daffi import Client, callback, TCPTransport

@callback
def process(task: str) -> str:
    return f"done: {task}"

client = Client(app_name="worker-1", transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6000))
client.connect()
client.join()  # block until Ctrl+C / SIGTERM
  1. Create a caller.

caller.py:

from daffi import Client, TCPTransport

client = Client(app_name="caller", transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6000))
conn = client.connect()

# RPC — routed to one worker (round-robin if many workers expose the same function)
result = conn.rpc().process("job-42")

# Cast — sent to all workers, returns {worker_name: result}
all_results = conn.cast().process("broadcast-job")

client.stop()

docs.title: What just happened?
docs.text:
1. The listener (Service or Router) starts accepting connections on the transport.
  2. @callback registers functions at import time; they are advertised during the handshake.
  3. Client.connect() completes the handshake and returns a connection handle.
  4. conn.rpc() / conn.cast() return proxies — attribute access invokes the remote function.

docs.title: Async interface (daffi.aio)
docs.text:
daffi.aio is an asyncio-native interface that mirrors the synchronous Daffi API. OS threads are replaced with coroutines, blocking calls with await, and the event loop is never blocked.

All public methods (connect, start, join, stop) are async def. Callbacks can be regular functions or async def coroutines.

The native runtime (threads / evented) is independent of daffi.aio — both models work with the async interface. See Native runtime.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Service (direct)Router + Worker 
# 1_service.py
import asyncio
from daffi import callback, TCPTransport
from daffi.aio import AsyncService

@callback
async def multiply(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a * b

async def main():
    svc = AsyncService(
        app_name="calc-service",
        transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6001),
    )
    await svc.start()
    await svc.join()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

# 2_caller.py
import asyncio
from daffi import TCPTransport
from daffi.aio import AsyncClient

async def main():
    client = AsyncClient(
        app_name="calc-caller",
        transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6001),
    )
    conn = await client.connect()

    result = await conn.rpc(timeout=5).multiply(6, 7)
    print(result)  # → 42

    await client.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

# 1_router.py
import asyncio
from daffi import TCPTransport
from daffi.aio import AsyncRouter

async def main():
    router = AsyncRouter(transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6001))
    await router.start()
    await router.join()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

# 2_worker.py
import asyncio
from daffi import callback, TCPTransport
from daffi.aio import AsyncClient

@callback
async def multiply(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a * b

async def main():
    worker = AsyncClient(
        app_name="calc-worker",
        transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6001),
    )
    await worker.connect()
    await worker.join()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

# 3_caller.py
import asyncio
from daffi import TCPTransport
from daffi.aio import AsyncClient

async def main():
    caller = AsyncClient(
        app_name="calc-caller",
        transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6001),
    )
    conn = await caller.connect()

    result = await conn.rpc(timeout=5).multiply(6, 7)
    print(result)  # → 42

    await caller.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Classes
docs.text: Async class Sync equivalent Role AsyncClient Client Connect to a Router or Service; call remote callbacks; optionally expose your own. AsyncService Service Listen for incoming connections. AsyncRouter Router Forward messages between Clients.

docs.title: AsyncClient
docs.text:
from daffi import TCPTransport
from daffi.aio import AsyncClient

client = AsyncClient(
    app_name="my-client",
    workers=1,
    transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6001),
)

conn = await client.connect()
await client.join()
await client.stop()

Calls still waiting when the client stops raise Disconnected, as in the sync interface.

docs.title: Member events
docs.text:
on_member_added / on_member_removed handlers may be regular functions or async def coroutines. Coroutines run on the event loop; regular functions run on a worker thread, so they must not touch asyncio objects directly — use loop.call_soon_threadsafe.

loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
joined = asyncio.Event()

@conn.on_member_added
def _added(name: str):
    loop.call_soon_threadsafe(joined.set)

docs.title: workers
docs.text:
Value Behaviour 1 (default) One incoming callback at a time. N Up to N callbacks run concurrently, each in its own asyncio.Task.

Requests beyond the limit stay queued; once the queue is full, callers get ServiceOverloaded.

docs.title: AsyncService / AsyncRouter
docs.text:
from daffi.aio import AsyncService, AsyncRouter

svc = AsyncService(app_name="my-service", workers=4, transport=TCPTransport("0.0.0.0", 6001))
await svc.start()
await svc.join()
await svc.stop()

router = AsyncRouter(transport=TCPTransport("0.0.0.0", 6001))
await router.start()
await router.join()

docs.title: AsyncClientConnection
docs.text:
Proxy methods return awaitables — you must await each call.

from daffi import SerdeFormat

conn = await client.connect()

result = await conn.rpc(timeout=10).my_function(arg1, arg2)
results = await conn.cast(timeout=10).my_function(arg1)

await conn.rpc_nowait().my_function(arg1)
await conn.cast_nowait().my_function(arg1)

await conn.stream(serde=SerdeFormat.OPAQUE).process_stream(chunk_source("large.bin"))
await conn.stream_nowait(serde=SerdeFormat.OPAQUE).process_stream(chunk_source("large.bin"))

await conn.wait_for_members("worker-1", "worker-2", timeout=30)

docs.title: Async callbacks
docs.text:
from daffi import callback

@callback
def compute(n: int) -> int:
    return sum(range(n))

@callback
async def fetch(url: str) -> str:
    import aiohttp
    async with aiohttp.ClientSession() as session:
        async with session.get(url) as resp:
            return await resp.text()

Warning

An async def callback cannot be used with the synchronous Client / Service / Router — it raises TypeError at call time. Use daffi.aio components for async callbacks.

docs.title: Communication patterns
docs.text:
All six call styles work like the sync interface, with await added:

Style Async usage Returns rpc() await conn.rpc(timeout=N).fn(args) Single result rpc_nowait() await conn.rpc_nowait().fn(args) None once sent cast() await conn.cast(timeout=N).fn(args) {name: result} dict cast_nowait() await conn.cast_nowait().fn(args) None once sent stream() await conn.stream(serde=…).fn(iterator) None stream_nowait() await conn.stream_nowait(serde=…).fn(iterator) None once sent

See Communication patterns and Serialization.

docs.title: Concurrent I/O with asyncio.gather
docs.text:
Fire many RPCs concurrently without OS threads:

import asyncio
from daffi import TCPTransport
from daffi.aio import AsyncClient

async def main():
    clients = [
        AsyncClient(app_name=f"caller-{i}", transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6001))
        for i in range(100)
    ]
    conns = await asyncio.gather(*[c.connect() for c in clients])

    results = await asyncio.gather(*[
        conn.rpc(timeout=10).process(i)
        for i, conn in enumerate(conns)
    ])

    await asyncio.gather(*[c.stop() for c in clients])

async def callbacks that perform I/O yield the event loop while waiting, so other tasks continue uninterrupted.

docs.title: When to use sync vs async
docs.text: Workload Recommendation Sequential scripts, one call at a time Sync — simpler, lower per-call overhead Many concurrent callers Async — cooperative scheduling without OS threads I/O-bound callbacks (DB, HTTP, file I/O) Async — async def callbacks yield the loop CPU-bound callbacks Either — GIL limits both; use multiple worker processes Mixed async codebase (FastAPI, aiohttp, …) Async — no run_in_executor needed for the Daffi surface

docs.title: Mixing sync and async
docs.text:
• An async def callback used with a sync Client raises TypeError.
  • A sync def callback used with AsyncClient is offloaded to a ThreadPoolExecutor.

If you need both sync and async nodes in the same process, run the async components inside asyncio.run() in a dedicated thread.

docs.title: Communication patterns
docs.text:
Daffi provides several communication patterns through the connection handle returned by client.connect().

conn = client.connect()

Each method returns a proxy that allows remote functions to be invoked through attribute access.

docs.title: RPC — rpc()
docs.text:
Execute a remote function and wait for its result.

In a Router topology, calls are distributed across matching workers using round-robin selection.

result = conn.rpc(timeout=5).echo("hello")

result = conn.rpc(
    timeout=5,
    serde=SerdeFormat.JSON,
).add(1, 2)

To target a specific worker, use receiver:

result = conn.rpc(
    timeout=5,
    receiver="worker-1",
).process("task")

receiver is only relevant when connecting through a Router with multiple workers. In the Service topology there is always exactly one receiver — the Service itself.

Option Type Default Description timeout float \| None None Seconds to wait. None waits forever. receiver str \| list[str] \| None None Pin to a specific node, or rotate among the listed names. serde SerdeFormat MSGPACK Serialization format.

docs.title: Fire-and-forget — rpc_nowait()
docs.text:
Invoke a remote function without waiting for its result.

conn.rpc_nowait().notify("event happened")
Option Type Default Description receiver str \| list[str] \| None None Pin to a specific node. serde SerdeFormat MSGPACK Serialization format.

docs.title: Broadcast — cast()
docs.text:
Execute a remote function on all matching workers and collect their results.

The returned dictionary maps worker names to their respective results.

results = conn.cast(timeout=5).echo("ping")

# Example:
# {
#     "worker-01": "ping",
#     "worker-02": "ping",
# }

Restrict the broadcast with receiver:

results = conn.cast(
    timeout=5,
    receiver=["worker-A", "worker-C"],
).process("payload")

When using cast() against a single Service, the dict has exactly one entry.

Option Type Default Description timeout float \| None None Per-worker timeout. receiver str \| list[str] \| None None Restrict to these worker names. None = all. serde SerdeFormat MSGPACK Serialization format.

docs.title: Broadcast without waiting — cast_nowait()
docs.text:
Broadcast a function call without collecting results.

conn.cast_nowait().notify("broadcast event")
Option Type Default Description receiver str \| list[str] \| None None Restrict to these worker names. None = all. serde SerdeFormat MSGPACK Serialization format.

docs.title: Streaming — stream()
docs.text:
Send data in chunks with backpressure.

The sender waits for acknowledgement before sending the next chunk. The callback's return value is discarded; only the acknowledgement matters. Defaults to SerdeFormat.OPAQUE.

@callback
def process_stream(data: bytes) -> None:
    ...


# Split a large payload into fixed-size chunks (e.g. 64 KiB)
payload = open("large.bin", "rb").read()
chunks = [payload[i:i + 65536] for i in range(0, len(payload), 65536)]

sender = conn.stream(serde=SerdeFormat.OPAQUE)

for chunk in chunks:
    sender.process_stream(chunk)

Or pass an iterator / generator directly — stream() consumes it and sends each yielded value:

def chunk_source(path: str, size: int = 65536):
    with open(path, "rb") as f:
        while chunk := f.read(size):
            yield chunk


conn.stream(serde=SerdeFormat.OPAQUE).process_stream(
    chunk_source("large.bin"),
)
Option Type Default Description receiver str \| None None Pin to a specific worker. None picks one round-robin. serde SerdeFormat OPAQUE Serialization format for each chunk. timeout float \| None None Seconds to wait per chunk ack.

docs.title: Streaming without waiting — stream_nowait()
docs.text:
Send streaming data without waiting for acknowledgements.

conn.stream_nowait(serde=SerdeFormat.OPAQUE).process_stream(
    chunk_source("large.bin"),
)

No backpressure

The service queues incoming chunks as fast as the network delivers them. If the producer outpaces the consumer, messages accumulate until OS-level TCP flow control stalls the sender.

Option Type Default Description receiver str \| None None Pin to a specific worker. None picks one round-robin. serde SerdeFormat OPAQUE Serialization format for each chunk.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Method Target Returns Blocks? rpc() One worker (RR or pinned) Single result Yes rpc_nowait() One worker (RR or pinned) None No cast() All matching workers {name: result} dict Yes cast_nowait() All matching workers None No stream() One worker (RR or pinned) None Yes per chunk (backpressure) stream_nowait() One worker (RR or pinned) None No (no backpressure)

docs.title: Callbacks and concurrency
docs.text: Callbacks are Python functions or bound methods that can be invoked remotely by other nodes.

docs.title: Defining callbacks
docs.text:
Use the @callback decorator to register a remotely callable function.

from daffi import callback


@callback
def echo(payload):
    return payload


@callback
def compute(x: int, y: int) -> int:
    return x * y

Callback registration happens at import time.

Both Service and Client instances can expose callbacks.

docs.title: Class callbacks
docs.text:
Apply @callback to an entire class. Daffi instantiates it (no-argument constructor) and registers every public method as a remote callback.

Rules:

  • Methods whose names start with _ are skipped.
  • Methods decorated with @local are excluded — they remain local only.
  • All other public methods become remotely callable.
from daffi import callback
from daffi.registry import local


@callback
class TextProcessor:
    def __init__(self):
        self._call_count = 0

    def upper(self, text: str) -> str:
        self._call_count += 1
        return text.upper()

    def reverse(self, text: str) -> str:
        return text[::-1]

    @local
    def reset(self):
        """Not exported — only callable within this process."""
        self._call_count = 0

The class must be constructable with no arguments when decorated at class level. If you need constructor arguments, initialise the object first and decorate its methods individually.

docs.title: Concurrent callback execution
docs.text:
By default, each node executes incoming callbacks sequentially using a single execution thread:

workers=1

To execute multiple callbacks concurrently, configure the workers parameter.

import time

from daffi import Service, callback, TCPTransport


@callback
def slow_task(n: int) -> int:
    time.sleep(1)
    return n * n


svc = Service(
    workers=4,
    transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 5000),
)

svc.start()
svc.join()

With workers=4, up to four callbacks can execute concurrently.

The same parameter is available on a Client acting as a worker:

client = Client(
    app_name="worker-1",
    workers=8,
    transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6000),
)

docs.title: Choosing the right worker count
docs.text:
• I/O-bound callbacks: Increasing workers can improve concurrency when callbacks perform network requests, database queries, or file operations.
  • Lightweight callbacks: Keep workers=1 when sequential execution is sufficient.
  • CPU-bound callbacks: Python's GIL limits parallel execution of Python bytecode within a single process. Prefer multiple worker processes behind a Router for CPU-intensive workloads.

See Direct topology and Router and workers for how workers fits each topology.

docs.title: Event handlers
docs.text:
Daffi provides event handlers for monitoring changes in network membership.

Register handlers with on_member_added and on_member_removed to receive notifications when nodes connect or disconnect. Each handler receives the peer's app_name as a string.

Both Service and Client support these methods. They can be used as decorators or as plain method calls. Register handlers before start() / connect().

docs.title: Registering handlers
docs.text:
from daffi import Service, TCPTransport


svc = Service(
    transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 5000),
)


@svc.on_member_added
def on_join(member: str) -> None:
    print(f"connected: {member}")


@svc.on_member_removed
def on_leave(member: str) -> None:
    print(f"disconnected: {member}")


svc.start()
svc.join()

Or register without decorators:

def on_join(member: str) -> None:
    print(f"connected: {member}")

svc.on_member_added(on_join)

Multiple handlers can be registered; they run in registration order.

docs.title: Handlers
docs.text:
Method Description on_member_added Called when a node joins the network. Receives app_name. on_member_removed Called when a node leaves the network. Receives app_name.

Event handlers are useful for monitoring network membership, tracking worker availability, and implementing application-level lifecycle logic.

For waiting until specific peers appear before calling them, prefer conn.wait_for_members(...) — see Router and workers.

docs.title: Service-side example
docs.text:
from daffi import Service, callback, TCPTransport

@callback
def ping(msg: str) -> str:
    return f"pong: {msg}"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    connected: set[str] = set()

    svc = Service(app_name="event-service", transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 5009))

    @svc.on_member_added
    def on_join(member: str) -> None:
        connected.add(member)
        print(f"{member!r} connected (total: {len(connected)})")

    @svc.on_member_removed
    def on_leave(member: str) -> None:
        connected.discard(member)
        print(f"{member!r} disconnected (total: {len(connected)})")

    svc.start()
    svc.join()

docs.title: Router and workers
docs.text: The Router topology decouples callers from workers. The Router is a pure message forwarder; Workers register their callbacks with it; Callers invoke those callbacks through it.

docs.title: 1. Start the Router
docs.text:
The Router has no callbacks of its own — it only forwards messages.

from daffi import Router, TCPTransport

if __name__ == "__main__":
    router = Router(transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6001))
    router.start()
    print("Router running on 127.0.0.1:6001 — press Ctrl+C to stop.")
    router.join()

docs.title: Router parameters
docs.text:
Parameter Type Description transport transport or sequence One TCPTransport or UnixTransport, or several. Every listener shares this router's membership. start() brings all of them up at once or none of them. TLS is set on each TCPTransport. runtime Runtime THREADS or EVENTED for this process. Omit for threads. One process, one choice. auth_token str Shared secret. Every peer must send the same token in its handshake. A peer without it is disconnected before it can call anything. Omit to accept any peer.

Requests are only accepted from peers that have completed the handshake, under the name they registered. A request that names another peer as its sender is answered with UnknownSender. A reply is only accepted from the peer the request was routed to.

To listen on TCP and Unix together (remote peers + co-located processes), pass a list of transports — see Transports.

docs.title: 2. Connect Workers
docs.text:
Workers are Clients that expose @callback functions. Start as many instances as you need — the Router load-balances across them.

from daffi import Client, callback, TCPTransport

@callback
def multiply(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a * b

if __name__ == "__main__":
    worker = Client(app_name="calc-worker", transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6001))
    worker.connect()
    print("Worker connected — press Ctrl+C to stop.")
    worker.join()

Tip

Run two instances of this script in separate terminals. rpc() will round-robin between them; cast() will call both.

Each worker Client accepts the same workers parameter as Service for in-process callback concurrency. For CPU-bound work, prefer multiple worker processes behind the Router rather than raising workers on one process — see Callbacks and concurrency.

import os
from daffi import Client, TCPTransport

# Start N instances — one per core. The Router load-balances across them.
worker = Client(
    app_name=f"cpu-worker-{os.getpid()}",
    workers=1,
    transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6001),
)
worker.connect()
worker.join()

docs.title: 3. Connect a Caller
docs.text:
Callers are also Clients — they just don't expose any @callback functions.

from daffi import Client, TCPTransport

if __name__ == "__main__":
    caller = Client(app_name="calc-caller", transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6001))
    conn = caller.connect()

    # Round-robin — any available worker handles this call.
    result = conn.rpc(timeout=5).multiply(6, 7)
    print(f"multiply(6, 7) = {result}")  # → 42

    # Pin to a specific worker by name.
    result = conn.rpc(timeout=5, receiver="calc-worker").multiply(3, 3)

    caller.stop()

docs.title: Bidirectional communication
docs.text:
Because every Client can both expose callbacks and call remote ones, bidirectional communication is natural: two nodes connect to the same Router and call each other.

# node_a.py
from daffi import Client, callback, TCPTransport

@callback
def hello_from_a(msg: str) -> str:
    return f"A received: {msg}"

node_a = Client(app_name="node-A", transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6003))
conn = node_a.connect()

reply = conn.rpc(timeout=5, receiver="node-B").hello_from_b("hi from A")
print(reply)

# node_b.py
from daffi import Client, callback, TCPTransport

@callback
def hello_from_b(msg: str) -> str:
    return f"B received: {msg}"

node_b = Client(app_name="node-B", transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6003))
conn = node_b.connect()
node_b.join()

docs.title: cast() via Router
docs.text:
cast() fans out to every worker that exposes the requested function and collects all results.

conn = caller.connect()

results = conn.cast(timeout=5).process("task-A")
# → {"worker-1": result, "worker-2": result, ...}

results = conn.cast(timeout=5, receiver=["worker-1"]).process("task-B")

conn.cast_nowait().process("task-C")

See Communication patterns for the full comparison of call styles.

docs.title: Waiting for members
docs.text:
In a multi-worker environment the caller often starts before all workers are online. Use conn.wait_for_members() to block until the required peers appear:

from daffi import Client, TCPTransport

caller = Client(app_name="calc-caller", transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6001))
conn = caller.connect()

# Block until both workers have registered — start order doesn't matter.
conn.wait_for_members("worker-1", "worker-2")

results = conn.cast(timeout=10).process("task")
caller.stop()

An optional timeout raises TimeoutError if the deadline is exceeded:

conn.wait_for_members("slow-worker", timeout=30)
Parameter Type Default Description *members str — One or more peer names to wait for. timeout float \| None None Max seconds to wait. None waits forever.

docs.title: Native runtime
docs.text:
Daffi's compiled core supports two connection-handling models, configurable through the runtime argument.

The model only changes how the native core waits for network data. Callbacks, call styles, serialization formats, and the Python API are the same in both models.

Not the same as daffi.aio

daffi.aio is the Python asyncio API. The native runtime decides how the compiled core waits for sockets. The two are independent — daffi.aio works with either model.

docs.title: Runtime modes
docs.text: Runtime Description threads Creates an operating-system thread for each connection. Default runtime. evented Multiplexes connections across a small number of event-loop threads. Uses epoll on Linux and kqueue on macOS.

docs.title: Selecting a runtime
docs.text:
The runtime is selected once per process by the runtime argument of any Router, Service, or Client. Omitting runtime selects threads. A process cannot mix the two models; conflicting initialization raises InitializationError.

from daffi import Runtime, Router, TCPTransport

router = Router(
    transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6000),
    runtime=Runtime.EVENTED,
)

"threads" / "evented" are also accepted in place of the enum. Check which runtime is active:

from daffi import dfcore

print(dfcore.getRuntime())  # "evented" or "threads"
Argument Values Default runtime Runtime.THREADS, Runtime.EVENTED (or "threads", "evented") threads

A process started with spawn does not inherit the parent's lock — pass runtime into that process too. A child created with fork after Daffi has started keeps the runtime the parent already chose.

docs.title: Event-loop configuration
docs.text:
Use the DAFFI_EVENT_LOOPS environment variable to configure the number of event-loop threads.

The default is one loop per CPU, capped at 64.

DAFFI_EVENT_LOOPS=4 python router.py

docs.title: Choosing a runtime
docs.text:
Use threads when:

  • Connections may be slow to read large messages or streams. In the evented model a stalled peer can briefly hold up other connections on the same loop.
  • Your application primarily uses connections that benefit from independent thread handling.
  • Most clients are browsers (WebSocket). WebSocket sessions keep a dedicated thread in both models.

Use evented when:

  • A Router or Service needs to maintain many simultaneous connections.
  • Native thread count is a limiting resource (containers with a low pids limit, small memory requests).
  • Most connections are idle, such as workers waiting for tasks.
  • One process opens many Client connections.

If you are unsure, keep the default. Switch a Router or Service to evented when thread count grows with the number of connections and that becomes a problem. Nothing else in your code needs to change.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Event loops. A small fixed set of loop threads waits for socket readiness with kqueue (macOS/BSD) or epoll (Linux). Each new connection is assigned to a loop round-robin.
  • Incremental decoding. When a socket becomes readable, the loop reads available data and feeds it to a frame decoder. Complete messages are dispatched the same way as in the threaded model.
  • Blocking pool. Work that can block for a long time (TLS handshake, protocol probe, WebSocket sessions) never runs on a loop thread. It runs on an elastic pool so a silent peer cannot delay other connections.
  • Shutdown. stop() behaves the same in both models. It returns once every connection is closed and native resources are released.

The evented model is available on macOS and Linux.

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
Daffi supports multiple serialization formats, allowing applications to choose between interoperability, readability, flexibility, and performance.

Specify the desired format using serde=SerdeFormat.X on a communication method.

Format Description Typical use case MSGPACK Compact binary serialization. Default format. General-purpose communication JSON Human-readable, JSON-compatible data. Interoperability and debugging OPAQUE Raw bytes or strings without structured serialization. High-throughput data transfer PICKLE Python object serialization. Python-specific object exchange

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
from daffi import Client, SerdeFormat

conn = client.connect()

# MessagePack (default)
result = conn.rpc(timeout=5).add(1, 2)

# JSON
result = conn.rpc(
    timeout=5,
    serde=SerdeFormat.JSON,
).add(1, 2)

# Opaque binary data
result = conn.rpc(
    timeout=5,
    serde=SerdeFormat.OPAQUE,
).receive_data(binary_payload)

docs.title: MSGPACK (default)
docs.text: Binary MessagePack encoding — more compact than JSON, with the same basic type support (dict, list, str, int, float, bool, None). Cross-language. Required dependency of Daffi.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text: Language-agnostic. Works with plain Python types that are JSON-compatible. Prefer JSON when interoperating with non-Python processes or when human-readable payloads help debugging.

docs.title: OPAQUE
docs.text: Passes raw bytes or strings through without structured serialization. Use for custom binary protocols, pre-encoded payloads, or streaming large binary chunks. Both stream() and stream_nowait() default to OPAQUE.

docs.title: PICKLE
docs.text:
Python-native serialization. Supports arbitrary Python objects — dataclasses, Enums, custom classes — as long as both sides share the same class definitions. Not cross-language.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from daffi import Client, SerdeFormat, TCPTransport

@dataclass
class Order:
    order_id: str
    amount: float

client = Client(transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 5004))
conn = client.connect()

order = Order(order_id="ORD-001", amount=99.95)
result = conn.rpc(timeout=5, serde=SerdeFormat.PICKLE).process_order(order)

docs.title: Pickle serialization and security
docs.text:
Deserializing untrusted pickle data can execute arbitrary code. Only use it when the sender and transmitted data are trusted.

Daffi provides a receiver-side deserialization policy. The default serdes= is SerdeFormat.ALL (includes PICKLE). Pass serdes=SerdeFormat.SAFE to refuse pickle:

from daffi import Service, SerdeFormat, TCPTransport

svc = Service(
    app_name="public-service",
    serdes=SerdeFormat.SAFE,  # refuses PICKLE
    transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 5004),
)

A request in a format outside serdes= is answered with SerdeNotAllowed and never decoded.

PICKLE from a WebSocket peer is always refused: any web page can open a WebSocket to a server on the user's machine.

Warning

Do not treat serialization format selection as a substitute for authentication or trust validation. Prefer serdes=SerdeFormat.SAFE together with auth_token= and TLS when peers are not fully trusted.

docs.title: Format comparison
docs.text: Format Cross-language Arbitrary Python objects Binary MSGPACK Yes No Yes JSON Yes No No OPAQUE Yes No Yes PICKLE No Yes Yes

docs.title: Direct topology (Service)
docs.text:
The simplest Daffi topology: a Service hosts @callback functions; Clients call them.

Callbacks in the Service vs Router topology

In this topology Clients are typically pure callers — they connect to the Service and issue remote calls.

If you need Clients that also expose @callback functions (workers) or peers that call each other, use the Router topology instead.

docs.title: Service
docs.text:
from daffi import Service, callback, TCPTransport

@callback
def add(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return a + b

@callback
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f"Hello, {name}!"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    svc = Service(
        app_name="calc-service",
        transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 5001),
    )
    svc.start()
    print("Service running — press Ctrl+C to stop.")
    svc.join()

docs.title: Service parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description app_name str Unique name for this node. Auto-generated if omitted. transport transport or sequence One TCPTransport or UnixTransport, or several. Every listener shares this node's membership. start() brings all of them up at once or none of them. TLS is set on each TCPTransport. workers int Concurrency level for callback execution. Default: 1 (sequential). See Callbacks and concurrency. runtime Runtime THREADS or EVENTED for this process. Omit for threads. See Native runtime. auth_token str Shared secret every client must send in its handshake. Omit to accept any client. serdes SerdeFormat Receiver-side deserialization policy. Default: ALL. Pass SAFE to refuse PICKLE. See Serialization. callbacks list The @callback functions (or their names) this node offers. Default: every registered callback.

docs.title: Client
docs.text:
from daffi import Client, TCPTransport

if __name__ == "__main__":
    client = Client(app_name="calc-client", transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 5001))
    conn = client.connect()

    result = conn.rpc(timeout=5).add(3, 4)
    print(f"add(3, 4) = {result}")  # → 7

    conn.rpc_nowait().greet("world")

    client.stop()

docs.title: Client parameters
docs.text: Parameter Type Description app_name str Unique name for this node. transport TCPTransport or UnixTransport The one address this client connects to. runtime Runtime THREADS or EVENTED for this process. Omit for threads. auth_token str The token of a server started with auth_token=. workers int Concurrency for incoming callbacks when this Client acts as a worker. callbacks list For a client acting as a worker: the callbacks it offers. Default: every registered callback. serdes SerdeFormat Receiver-side deserialization policy.

docs.title: Calling the Service
docs.text:
conn = client.connect()

# Blocking call
result = conn.rpc(timeout=5).add(3, 4)

# Fire-and-forget
conn.rpc_nowait().greet("world")

# Broadcast — one entry when only one Service is running
results = conn.cast(timeout=5).add(1, 2)

# Stream chunks (see Communication patterns)
conn.stream(serde=SerdeFormat.OPAQUE).process_stream(chunk_source("large.bin"))

Full option tables for every call style: Communication patterns.

docs.title: Class callbacks
docs.text:
Apply @callback to an entire class to export its public methods. Methods starting with _ and methods marked @local are not exported.

from daffi import Service, callback, TCPTransport
from daffi.registry import local


@callback
class TextProcessor:
    def upper(self, text: str) -> str:
        return text.upper()

    def reverse(self, text: str) -> str:
        return text[::-1]

    @local
    def reset(self):
        pass


if __name__ == "__main__":
    svc = Service(app_name="text-service", transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 5003))
    svc.start()
    svc.join()

See Callbacks and concurrency for rules and workers guidance.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Daffi supports TLS encryption for TCP connections.

TLS allows clients to verify the server's identity and protects communication against network interception.

cert, key, and ca accept either a filesystem path or the PEM material itself. The native layer treats a value that starts with -----BEGIN as PEM and loads it from memory; anything else is a path.

docs.title: TLS configuration
docs.text:
Configure TLS on the server-side transport:

from daffi import Router, TCPTransport

router = Router(
    transport=TCPTransport(
        "127.0.0.1",
        6000,
        tls=True,
        cert="/path/to/server.crt",
        key="/path/to/server.key",
    ),
)

router.start()

Configure the Client with the trusted CA certificate:

from daffi import Client, TCPTransport

client = Client(
    transport=TCPTransport(
        "127.0.0.1",
        6000,
        tls=True,
        ca="/path/to/ca.crt",
    ),
)

conn = client.connect()

Inline PEM works the same way:

TCPTransport(
    "0.0.0.0",
    5443,
    tls=True,
    cert=open("server.crt").read(),
    key=open("server.key").read(),
)

Different listeners may use different TLS settings — for example TLS on TCP and plaintext on a Unix socket. See Transports.

docs.title: Certificate configuration
docs.text:
Parameter Role Description tls=True Both Enable TLS on this transport. cert Server / client Path or PEM for the local certificate (server identity, or client identity for mTLS). key Server / client Path or PEM for the local private key. ca Server / client Path or PEM for the peer trust store. On a listener, non-empty ca enables mutual TLS. On a client, the trust store used to verify the server. Empty on the client = the system trust store. verify Client True (default) verifies the server. False accepts any certificate: traffic is encrypted, but anyone on the path can impersonate the server.

These options live on TCPTransport / UnixTransport, not on Router / Service / Client.

Security recommendation: Configure certificate verification in production. Disabling server certificate verification exposes connections to man-in-the-middle attacks.

docs.title: Mutual TLS
docs.text:
Set ca on the listening transport and give the client matching cert / key (and usually the same ca to verify the server):

# Server — require client certificates
Service(
    transport=TCPTransport(
        "0.0.0.0", 5443,
        tls=True,
        cert=server_cert, key=server_key,
        ca=client_ca,
    ),
)

# Client — present an identity the server trusts
Client(
    transport=TCPTransport(
        "127.0.0.1", 5443,
        tls=True,
        ca=server_ca,
        cert=client_cert, key=client_key,
    ),
)

A self-signed setup can use one certificate as server identity, client identity, and CA on both sides.

docs.title: Generating self-signed certificates (development)
docs.text:
# Generate CA key + cert
openssl genrsa -out ca.key 4096
openssl req -new -x509 -days 3650 -key ca.key -out ca.crt -subj "/CN=daffi-ca"

# Generate server key + cert signed by the CA
openssl genrsa -out server.key 2048
openssl req -new -key server.key -out server.csr -subj "/CN=127.0.0.1"
openssl x509 -req -days 365 -in server.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key \
    -CAcreateserial -out server.crt

Use ca.crt as the ca on the client side. A self-signed certificate is not in the system trust store, so a client without ca refuses it; pass verify=False only for throwaway local testing.

docs.title: Related security controls
docs.text:
• auth_token= — shared secret checked during the handshake. On TCP, using auth_token requires tls=True.
  • serdes=SerdeFormat.SAFE — refuse pickle deserialization on the receiver. See Serialization.

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
Daffi supports multiple transport mechanisms for communication between processes.

Client accepts a single transport. Router and Service accept one transport or a sequence of them — every listener shares that node's membership, and start() brings all of them up together.

docs.title: TCP
docs.text:
Use TCPTransport to communicate between processes over a network or localhost.

from daffi import Service, Client, TCPTransport

svc = Service(
    transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 5000),
)
svc.start()

client = Client(
    transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 5000),
)
conn = client.connect()

docs.title: Unix domain sockets
docs.text:
Use UnixTransport for inter-process communication on the same machine, without binding a TCP port.

Platform support

Unix sockets are supported on Linux and macOS only.

from daffi import Service, Client, UnixTransport

svc = Service(
    transport=UnixTransport("/tmp/daffi.sock"),
)
svc.start()

client = Client(
    transport=UnixTransport("/tmp/daffi.sock"),
)
conn = client.connect()

The API is identical to TCP — only the transport constructor changes.

docs.title: Existing socket files
docs.text: start() removes a socket file left behind by a server that is gone. It refuses to start, and leaves the path alone, when the path is something other than a socket, or a socket another server is still accepting on.

docs.title: Multiple transports
docs.text:
A common pattern is to expose both TCP (for remote clients or workers) and a Unix socket (for processes on the same host):

from daffi import Router, Client, TCPTransport, UnixTransport

tcp = TCPTransport("0.0.0.0", 6000)
unix = UnixTransport("/tmp/daffi.sock")

router = Router(
    transport=[tcp, unix],
)
router.start()

# Remote worker connects over TCP
remote = Client(
    app_name="worker-remote",
    transport=TCPTransport("127.0.0.1", 6000),
)
remote.connect()

# Co-located client connects over the Unix socket
local = Client(
    app_name="worker-local",
    transport=UnixTransport("/tmp/daffi.sock"),
)
local.connect()

Listeners may also use different TLS settings — for example TLS on TCP and plaintext on a Unix socket. See Security.

docs.title: Choosing a transport
docs.text: Transport Use when TCP Communication between processes on the same or different machines Unix sockets Local inter-process communication Both TCP for remote peers, Unix for co-located clients or workers
